title: Hidden, Disabled or Read-Only?
intro: Three states, three meanings. Pick by asking what the user should know about the feature, not by what is easiest to build.

learn.title: Three states, three meanings
learn.text:
**Hidden** — this user can never use it.
**Read-only** — a value the system makes, or one edited somewhere else.
**Disabled** — it exists, but this user can’t use it right now.

The choice is a product decision. It tells people what the product is and what they can expect from it.

try.q: A field shows an account ID the system generates. Users change it nowhere. Which state fits?
options: Read-only, with a hint if editable elsewhere
Disabled, with a note about why it is greyed out
Hidden, since nobody can change it anyway
Editable, with validation on every keystroke
try.explain: The value is system-made, so people can see it but not edit it. Add a hint where it can be changed, if anywhere.

left.label: Hide it when
items: The user can never use it
It is irrelevant to their role

right.label: Disable it when
items: The user may use it later

learn.title: Ask the first question first
learn.text:
Before choosing a state, ask: **should this feature be limited at all?**

It may be irrelevant, not allowed for this role, or temporarily unavailable. Each leads somewhere different.

If the user can never interact with it, hide it — but still decide when, how and to whom it appears, so the product doesn’t look inconsistent between roles.

try.q: A Delete button is irrelevant to the Viewer role, which can never delete. What fits best?
options: Hide it, and plan how it appears elsewhere
Disable it and explain why in a tooltip
Make it read-only for this role
Show it with a warning when pressed
try.explain: If a user can never use something, a disabled control only teaches them to hunt for a way to unlock it.

learn.title: A disabled control needs a reason
learn.text:
A disabled control must say **why** and **what unlocks it**: a missing permission, a missing prerequisite, a temporary state.

WCAG 2.2 AA doesn’t require contrast on disabled controls, but people still need to read them. Keep the text legible and, ideally, focusable so a screen reader announces the reason.

**Never hide buttons or filters by default.** People expect them to stay where they were.

try.q: Publish is unavailable until a title is added. What should the disabled button do?
options: Stay focusable and say a title is needed
Disappear until the title is filled in
Stay grey, with no explanation at all
Turn red and show an error on hover only
try.explain: The user needs the reason, and keyboard and screen-reader users need to reach it too.

test.q: What is the first question in the decision tree?
options: Should this be limited for this user at all?
Which colour should the disabled state use?
Is the thing a button, a field or a link?
Does the person use a touch device or a mouse?
test.explain: Hidden, read-only and disabled only make sense once you know why the feature is limited.

test.q: When should a feature be hidden?
options: When this user can never use it
When it is temporarily unavailable
When it needs a prerequisite first
When it takes up too much space
test.explain: Temporary or conditional limits call for disabled with a reason. Hiding is for things that are never theirs.

test.q: Read-only fits best for which of these?
options: A value the system makes or edits elsewhere
A button the user has no permission for
A feature that is outside the customer’s plan
A field that currently shows an error
test.explain: Read-only shows a value people need to see but can’t change here. Add a hint pointing to where it can be edited.

test.q: What must every disabled control include?
options: The reason, and what unlocks it
Lower contrast than any enabled control
Removal from the keyboard tab order
A tooltip that shows on mouse hover only
test.explain: A disabled control with no reason reads as a bug. Hover-only text is invisible on touch screens and to keyboard users.

test.q: A filter has no effect on the current results. What should the interface do by default?
options: Keep it visible where it was
Remove it until it applies again
Hide it until the user hovers nearby
Move it into an overflow menu instead
test.explain: Buttons and filters that move or vanish make people doubt the interface. Keep them in place, and disable with a reason if needed.
